title: Publication and dedication
short: Printed in Survey Graphic (March 1925) and in Color (1925), where it is dedicated to Harold Jackman; Cullen's best-known long poem.
body: Cullen (1903-1946) was still a student when 'Heritage' appeared in the Harlem number of Survey Graphic, edited by Alain Locke, in a version slightly different from the one collected that autumn in his first book, Color. The book version is dedicated to Harold Jackman, a Harlem schoolteacher and Cullen's closest friend. The poem was also included in Locke's anthology The New Negro (1925), and it became a central text in debates about what Africa could mean to Black Americans three centuries after the slave trade.

Alain Locke, ed., The New Negro: An Interpretation (Albert and Charles Boni, 1925)

Alan R. Shucard, Countee Cullen (Twayne, 1984)

title: The refrain question
short: The opening question returns as a refrain; the poem never answers it decisively.
body: The question frames the first section and returns in the middle of the poem (l. 63, closing a repeated stanza, ll. 60-63). Grammatically it can be dismissive ('What does Africa matter to me?') or searching ('What is Africa, for me?'). Critics have read the poem's oscillation between these senses as its subject: the speaker's attempts to dismiss Africa keep failing. The line may also recall Hamlet's 'What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba?' (Hamlet 2.2), another question about feeling for a distant cause.

Gerald Early, ed., My Soul's High Song: The Collected Writings of Countee Cullen (Anchor/Doubleday, 1991), introduction
William Shakespeare, Hamlet 2.2, the Hecuba soliloquy

title: Trochaic tetrameter couplets
short: Rhymed couplets of seven-syllable trochaic lines, the incantatory measure of Blake's 'Tyger' and Milton's 'L'Allegro'.
body: Most lines have four stresses beginning on a stressed syllable and lacking a final unstressed syllable ('COP-per SUN or SCAR-let SEA'). The measure is chant-like and drumming, appropriate to a poem about the 'throbbing' drums and rain that invade the speaker's body. Cullen, a deliberately traditional poet who admired Keats, uses an English form to explore an African theme, a tension central to the poem.

Houston A. Baker Jr., A Many-Colored Coat of Dreams: The Poetry of Countee Cullen (Broadside Press, 1974)
William Blake, 'The Tyger' (1794)

anchor: When the birds of Eden sang
title: Birds of Eden
short: Africa is imagined as Eden, the original paradise and, on some readings, humanity's cradle.
body: The line places the speaker's ancestors in a primal, paradisal past. Genesis locates Eden near rivers including Gihon, which 'compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia' (Genesis 2:13 KJV), so the identification has a biblical basis. The romantic image of Africa as a lost garden is part of the poem's self-consciously exotic vision, which the speaker later admits is 'A book one thumbs'.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Genesis 2:8-14
Gerald Early, ed., My Soul's High Song: The Collected Writings of Countee Cullen (Anchor/Doubleday, 1991), introduction

title: Three centuries removed
short: The speaker is separated from Africa by about three hundred years of slavery and life in America.
body: The first enslaved Africans recorded in English Virginia arrived in 1619, roughly three centuries before the poem. 'Removed' carries both the sense of distance in descent and of forcible transport. The impersonal 'One... his fathers' generalises the speaker into a representative African American. The phrase 'his fathers loved' assumes an ancestral attachment that the speaker cannot himself feel, which is the poem's problem from the start.

sources.cite: National Park Service, Historic Jamestowne, 'The 1619 landing'
Alan R. Shucard, Countee Cullen (Twayne, 1984)
Gerald Early, ed., My Soul's High Song: The Collected Writings of Countee Cullen (Anchor/Doubleday, 1991), introduction

title: Spicy grove, cinnamon tree
short: Stock exotic imagery of the tropics, recalling the Song of Songs and missionary hymnody.
body: Cinnamon is among the spices of the beloved's garden in the Song of Songs (4:14), and 'spicy breezes' blowing over Ceylon appear in Reginald Heber's missionary hymn 'From Greenland's Icy Mountains' (1819), widely sung in American churches. Whether or not Cullen intended the hymn echo, the line draws on a Western, partly missionary image of tropical lands; the irony is that the Christian speaker's idea of Africa is itself secondhand.

anchor: So I lie, who all day
title: 'So I lie'
short: A pun: the speaker lies down listening, and tells a lie when he claims Africa means nothing to him.
body: 'Lie' can mean recline (he lies awake hearing the drums) or speak falsely. The repeated formula 'So I lie, who...' (ll. 11, 19, 23, 64, 71) introduces each admission that he cannot shut Africa out, so that the second sense exposes the first section's question as a pose. Most critics treat this pun as the key to the poem's irony.

title: Juggernauts
greek: Hindi Jagannath, from Sanskrit jagannatha, 'lord of the world'
short: Massive, irresistible forces; here herds of elephants or similar beasts trampling the grass.
body: The word comes from Hindi Jagannath, 'lord of the world', a form of Vishnu whose huge temple car at Puri was described by European writers as crushing devotees under its wheels. By the twentieth century it meant any overwhelming force. The jungle herds are imagined at an epic, unstoppable scale, part of the poem's lush, stylised Africa. The word's Indian origin also shows how freely the poem mixes exotic vocabularies.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'juggernaut, n.'
Alan R. Shucard, Countee Cullen (Twayne, 1984)

title: Plighting troth
short: Pledging faith in marriage; an archaic formula from the English marriage service.
body: 'Plight' means pledge and 'troth' means truth or fidelity; the phrase is familiar from the Book of Common Prayer ('and thereto I plight thee my troth'). Applied to 'young forest lovers', it gives the imagined African scene the dignity of Christian marriage while also marking the speaker's distance, since he describes African love in English liturgical terms. The phrase belongs to the speaker's fantasy of Africa.

anchor: Great drums throbbing through the air
title: The drums
short: He hears African drums even with his thumbs in his ears: the heritage is in his body, not in his choice.
body: The comic-desperate gesture of cramming thumbs into his ears shows that the 'sound' is internal. The drum was a central and much-romanticised symbol of Africa in Harlem Renaissance writing, and Cullen uses it to dramatise ancestral memory as pulse and blood. The next lines make the blood itself a 'dammed' tide pressing against the 'chafing net' of his veins. The image is comic as well.

sources.cite: Alan R. Shucard, Countee Cullen (Twayne, 1984)
Houston A. Baker Jr., A Many-Colored Coat of Dreams: The Poetry of Countee Cullen (Broadside Press, 1974)
George Hutchinson, The Harlem Renaissance in Black and White (Harvard University Press, 1995)

title: Primitivism
short: The poem's Africa of jungles, drums and 'barbaric' passion reflects 1920s primitivism; critics debate whether Cullen endorses or exposes it.
body: White and Black writers of the 1920s often imagined Africa as a realm of untamed instinct, opposed to 'civilized' restraint. Some critics fault 'Heritage' for repeating these stereotypes, since Cullen had never been to Africa; others argue that the poem presents them as fantasy ('A book one thumbs') and dramatises the American speaker's confusion. Langston Hughes's 1926 essay 'The Negro Artist and the Racial Mountain' famously criticised a young poet, generally identified as Cullen, for wanting to be 'a poet - not a Negro poet'.

Houston A. Baker Jr., A Many-Colored Coat of Dreams: The Poetry of Countee Cullen (Broadside Press, 1974)

title: Africa as a book
short: Africa, he claims, is only a book he reads listlessly until he sleeps, a secondhand, literary Africa.
body: The line attempts dismissal: Africa is a dull text, its beasts 'unremembered'. But the lush description that follows (bats, cats, the lion's 'bugle-throated roar', snakes, 'leprous flowers') contradicts the claim of boredom, so the denial undermines itself. 'Thumbs' links back to the thumbs in his ears (l. 21). The phrase also hints at the source of the speaker's Africa: travel writing, missionary literature and romance, rather than memory or experience.

sources.cite: Houston A. Baker Jr., A Many-Colored Coat of Dreams: The Poetry of Countee Cullen (Broadside Press, 1974)
Gerald Early, ed., My Soul's High Song: The Collected Writings of Countee Cullen (Anchor/Doubleday, 1991), introduction

anchor: From the scabbards where they slept
title: Claws in scabbards
short: The lion's claws are swords drawn from their sheaths; the 'bugle-throated roar' gives the image a military flourish.
body: A scabbard is a sheath for a sword. The metaphor makes the big cat's retractable claws into blades, and the 'monarch' is the lion, king of beasts. The heraldic, epic register shows Cullen's literary training: Africa is rendered through the conventions of English poetry. Lions sheathing their claws like swords give the jungle a chivalric dignity, which again shows Africa seen through European literary lenses rather than at first hand.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'scabbard, n.'

title: leprous flowers; corollas
short: Corollas are the whorls of petals of a flower; 'leprous' suggests mottled, diseased-looking blooms.
body: From Latin corolla, 'little crown or garland'. The adjective 'leprous' gives the tropical flowers a decadent, even sinister beauty, in the manner of fin-de-siecle poetry. The image belongs to the passage in which the speaker insists that 'Here', in America, no such things exist. 'Rear' (raise up) gives the flowers an aggressive, almost animal energy; even the vegetation, in this imagined Africa, is fierce and sensual.

title: Last year's snow
short: Echoes Villon's refrain 'Mais ou sont les neiges d'antan?' ('Where are the snows of yesteryear?'), the classic image of the vanished past.
body: Francois Villon's 'Ballade des dames du temps jadis', known in English through Dante Gabriel Rossetti's 'The Ballad of Dead Ladies', asks where the snows of past years have gone. Cullen turns the lament into a question of indifference: what is the past to me? The tree that 'must forget / How its past arose or set' offers a natural analogy for forgetting origins, but the poem's next movement shows that forgetting is impossible.

anchor: When the rain begins to fall
title: The rain
short: Rain stirs an ancestral dance in his body, crying 'Strip!' and 'Come and dance the Lover's Dance!'
body: The rain's 'weird refrain' and 'primal measures' are compared to a mad soul and a 'baited worm', strong images of compulsion and discomfort. The rain's voice urges him to shed the 'new exuberance', presumably his American, Christian, civilised self, for an 'old remembered way'. The passage most clearly dramatises the poem's idea of racial memory as bodily, an idea later critics have questioned as essentialist.

sources.cite: Alan R. Shucard, Countee Cullen (Twayne, 1984)
Houston A. Baker Jr., A Many-Colored Coat of Dreams: The Poetry of Countee Cullen (Broadside Press, 1974)
Gerald Early, ed., My Soul's High Song: The Collected Writings of Countee Cullen (Anchor/Doubleday, 1991), introduction

title: Conversion
short: The speaker belongs to Christ, but his conversion 'came high-priced', at the cost of slavery and the loss of ancestral gods.
body: The line is often read as an allusion to the slave trade: Christianity reached his ancestors through enslavement. Cullen, the adopted son of the Rev. Frederick A. Cullen, minister of Salem Methodist Episcopal Church in Harlem, writes from inside the church. The confident 'Heathen gods are naught to me' then echoes the refrain's pose of indifference and is undercut in the next section.

sources.cite: Gerald Early, ed., My Soul's High Song: The Collected Writings of Countee Cullen (Anchor/Doubleday, 1991), introduction
Alan R. Shucard, Countee Cullen (Twayne, 1984)
Countee Cullen, Collected Poems, ed. Major Jackson (Library of America, 2013), notes

title: The twice-turned cheek
short: Christ who taught 'turn to him the other also' (Matthew 5:39), the doctrine of non-resistance the speaker struggles to accept.
body: 'Twice-turned' compresses the command to turn the other cheek after the first has been struck. 'Lamb of God' (John 1:29) adds the image of the sacrificial victim. The speaker's 'idle boast' of faith is spoken 'with my mouth' while 'in my heart / Do I play a double part', echoing Isaiah 29:13 ('this people draw near me with their mouth... but have removed their heart far from me').

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Matthew 5:39; John 1:29; Isaiah 29:13
Houston A. Baker Jr., A Many-Colored Coat of Dreams: The Poetry of Countee Cullen (Broadside Press, 1974)

anchor: Lord, I fashion dark gods, too
title: A Black Christ
short: He wishes God were black, so that Christ would share the race's suffering, and imagines him with dark features and flashes of anger.
body: The idea of a Black Christ who bears 'a kindred woe' anticipates Cullen's long poem The Black Christ (1929). Here the speaker 'fashions dark gods' just as the 'heathen' do (ll. 85-86), which collapses his earlier contrast between pagan and Christian. His Christ has patience that 'wavers' and anger that rises to the 'smitten cheek'. The section ends with a plea for forgiveness that 'my need / Sometimes shapes a human creed', an admission that theology is shaped by experience.

sources.cite: Gerald Early, ed., My Soul's High Song: The Collected Writings of Countee Cullen (Anchor/Doubleday, 1991), introduction
Houston A. Baker Jr., A Many-Colored Coat of Dreams: The Poetry of Countee Cullen (Broadside Press, 1974)
Countee Cullen, The Black Christ and Other Poems (Harper and Brothers, 1929)

anchor: Lest I perish in the flood
title: Flood and fire
short: He must cool his blood lest it flood or ignite him; the images of flax and wax come from scripture.
body: The ending draws together the poem's blood-tide and fire imagery. 'Burning like the dryest flax' recalls Judges 15:14 and Isaiah 1:31, and 'Melting like the merest wax' Psalm 22:14 and 68:2 ('as wax melteth before the fire'). The 'hidden ember' in timber 'that I thought was wet' suggests that suppressed feeling can still catch fire. 'Lest the grave restore its dead' echoes Revelation 20:13, where 'the sea gave up the dead': the past might rise again.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Judges 15:14; Isaiah 1:31; Psalm 22:14; Psalm 68:2; Revelation 20:13
Alan R. Shucard, Countee Cullen (Twayne, 1984)

title: 'They and I are civilized'
short: The final irony: his heart and head have not yet 'realized' that he and they are civilised, so the conflict remains open.
body: 'They' are probably his heart and head, the faculties that have not accepted civilisation, though some readers take the word to mean his African ancestors. The flat closing word 'civilized' echoes contemporary arguments about 'civilized' and 'primitive' races and turns them back ironically. Critics differ on the tone: some find a confession of permanent division, others an ironic critique of the very idea of being civilised.
